replies.reply:
DO: I turn to Ambrose and say slow, "Ambrose. Three days, the little ones asleep, no shadows under the lamp. You keep the clock. Does it tick wrong since the toys came? Tell me what you know, and I'll pay you for it fair, a button if it's worth one."

JOURNAL: I can't sleep, and the children's hearths are cold. Ambrose knows the tower and the clock, so I ask him first and offer to pay so I don't end up owing him. I'm working toward finding why the children won't wake.

DO: I turn to Ambrose and say slow, "Three days, the little ones won't wake. You keep the clock, you'd know if it's wrong. Is the ticking off, Ambrose? Fast like this?" Then I wait on his answer and count the chain twitches while he talks.

JOURNAL: I can't sleep, and the clock's ticking loud and fast, and the children have no shadows. Ambrose is the one man who knows this tower, so I ask him plain before I spend a button on anything. I'm working toward finding why the children won't wake.

DO: I turn to Ambrose and say slow, "Three days, the little ones won't wake. You keep the clock, you'd know if something's off in it. Is the ticking wrong, Ambrose? Fast like this?" I keep my sock shut and don't ask for any favour I can't pay for.

JOURNAL: I can't sleep, and the clock's racing is the oddest thing about tonight, so I'll ask the man who keeps it before I spend a button on anything. I want to know why the children won't wake, and I'd rather learn it by asking plain than by owing.

DO: I pull my shawl tight and turn to Pip Pumbleton, since she's the only one here who's as wide awake as I am. "Goodness, Pip, you look like a coat buttoned up wrong! Tell me about your brother's shadow, properly, from the start. When did you last see it, and who was near him?"

JOURNAL: Pip is after the same trouble I am, shadows and sleeping children, and she's the one with an actual clue. I want to find out why the children won't wake, and if I'm the one who helps, perhaps people will finally look at me twice.

DO: I turn to Pip, who's standing stubborn as a hatpin under the lamp, and say, "Goodness, Pip, you look positively threadbare with worry. Tell me about your brother's shadow, properly, from the start. When did you last see it, and who was near him?" Then I glance at Mags and Dilly to see if either of them knows anything.

JOURNAL: Pip is the only one here with a real lead, since her brother's shadow is missing just like the sleeping children's. If I start with her, I might find out why the children won't wake, and maybe she'll think better of me for caring.

DO: I turn to Pip Pumbleton, sweep my shawl straight and say, "Goodness, Pip, you're wide awake in a night like this, aren't you? Tell me about your brother's shadow, and where you saw it last. I'll help you look, and I'm rather good at noticing things."

JOURNAL: Pip is the only one here with a real thread to pull, since she's after a missing shadow and the sleeping children cast none. If I help her I might learn why the children won't wake, and perhaps someone will finally notice me for it.

DO: Hop over to Pip with my pole on my shoulder and grin. "Chum, easy as winking, I'll help you find that shadow! First things first, what's it cost to get a look at your brother? Where did the toy come from, and has anyone got one left to look at?" Then I'll ask Mags if she's bought any of those wind-up toys off the children.

JOURNAL: Pip is the only one awake and she's after a missing shadow, which is the same riddle as the sleeping children, so she's my best lead. If I can get hold of one of those wind-up toys, I might be the one who cracks it, and everyone will know who did.

DO: Spin round to Pip with my pole over my shoulder and grin. "Easy as winking, chum! Before I say I'll fix anything, tell me straight: what's this about your brother's shadow? Where did you last see it, and which toy did he have from that peddler? And Mags, you've got ears all over this square, did you see which way the peddler went?"
JOURNAL: Children asleep with no shadows is the biggest thing I could ever fix, and everyone would know it was me. I need facts first, so I'm asking Pip about the shadow and the toy, and Mags about the peddler.

DO: Hop over to Pip with my pole on my shoulder and grin at her. "Chum, easy as winking, we'll get your brother's shadow back! Tell me first, where did you last see it, and what did that peddler's wind-up toy look like? Does Mags know what one of those toys might fetch?"

JOURNAL: Pip is the only one who's awake and chasing the same trouble I am, and the shadowless sleepers are the best clue I have. If I get the toy's story out of her, I can work out how to wake the children, and I'll be the one who fixed it.

DO: Pull my goggles down and head south down Crooked Lane, stopping at the drain halfway to kneel and peer into it with my notebook out, then on to Gloomer's Meadow to have a look at the peddler's wagon. "Hypothesis, my dear colleague: the drain knows something. Test: listen to it, then be ruder."

JOURNAL: The children cast no shadows and nobody else finds that strange, so I'll start with the drain I've always meant to look into, then the peddler's wagon where the toys came from. I'm working toward finding out how the sleeping is done, because what can be done can be undone.

DO: I flip my goggles down and head south down Crooked Lane toward Gloomer's Meadow, stopping first at that drain I've always meant to look into: crouch at the grate with my notebook, listen, and peer in for anything odd, then carry on to the peddler's wagon. "Hypothesis, my dear colleague: the drain knows something. Test: ask it nicely, then rudely."

JOURNAL: Children with no shadows is a puzzle nobody else will touch, and the drain and the peddler's wagon are the two places in town that the grown-ups avoid. I'm checking the nearer one first, for clues, before I confront the peddler with only four buttons and a notebook.

DO: Pull my goggles down and head south down Crooked Lane, stopping at the drain halfway to crouch and peer into it with my notebook out. "Hypothesis, my dear colleague: the drain knows something. Test: listen, then lower a button on a string and see what answers." Then on to Gloomer's Meadow to take a look at that peddler's wagon.

JOURNAL: Nobody else thinks the shadowless sleeping children need explaining, so I'll start with the two oddities closest at hand: the drain I've always meant to look into, and the peddler's wagon where the toys came from. If something can be done, it can be undone, and I mean to find out how.
